title: Caches & the Memory Hierarchy
summary: Why memory is a hierarchy, how CPU caches are organised and addressed, write policies and AMAT maths, writing cache-friendly code, coherence and false sharing on multicore, and how DRAM, NUMA and prefetching shape real performance.

lessons.title: Locality and the memory hierarchy
lessons.summary: The latency, capacity and cost trade-offs behind memory hierarchies, and how temporal and spatial locality help caches.
lessons.body:
Many high-performance CPU cores overlap several instructions. A dependent load missing all caches can stall work while DRAM responds; independent requests may overlap. Actual latency depends on the chip, workload and memory configuration.

Computers use a **hierarchy** to balance capacity, cost and latency: small memories close to execution units backed by larger levels. **Locality**, reuse of the same or nearby data, makes this arrangement effective.

## Why small memories can be fast

Three design costs motivate the hierarchy:

- **Distance.** Signals take time to cross a chip. A small memory sitting right next to the execution units can be read in a few cycles; a large one is physically further away and has longer wires.
- **Technology.** Many CPU caches are built from **SRAM**: each bit is a little latch of about six transistors. It is fast and needs no refresh, but it is big and expensive per bit. Main memory is **DRAM**: one transistor and one capacitor per bit. It is dense and cheap but slow, and it leaks (it must be refreshed, see the DRAM lesson).
- **Search cost.** Finding an item in a bigger structure takes more decoding and comparing, so even the same technology gets slower as it grows.

## The hierarchy in numbers

A common general-purpose hierarchy is shown below. Exact capacities and latencies require a named processor and measurement conditions; not every machine has every level. Register operands are not zero-time physical accesses, even when they add no separate cache-load instruction.

| Level | Role |
|---|---|
| Registers | Small operand storage near execution units |
| L1 | Small, low-latency instruction/data caches |
| L2 | More capacity with a different latency trade-off |
| L3 / last-level cache | Often shared across cores |
| DRAM | Main volatile storage |
| SSD | Persistent storage reached through I/O |

> Generic latency, cache-hit-rate and size ranges are omitted because no representative processor/workload measurements were verified for the earlier figures. Use specifications and measurements for the target machine.

```
       faster, smaller, dearer per byte
              ^
   [registers]
   [   L1   ]
   [    L2    ]
   [     L3     ]
   [     DRAM       ]
   [      SSD         ]
              v
       slower, bigger, cheaper per byte
```

> [!note] Where the OS fits in
> The operating system can cache file contents in DRAM (the page cache). Virtual memory and TLBs support address translation for memory accesses. Those are covered in the Operating Systems subject; here we focus on the CPU caches and DRAM.

## Locality: why a small cache works

If a program used every byte of its memory equally and at random, a 32 KiB cache in front of 16 GiB of DRAM would hit about 0.0002% of the time. Programs with useful locality can do much better than this independent uniform-access model. Two common forms of locality explain why.

### Temporal locality

**If you used something recently, you will probably use it again soon.** Loop counters, the top of the stack, a hot function's instructions, the root of a B-tree, a running total: all are touched over and over.

A cache exploits temporal locality by **keeping recently used data** and evicting data that has not been used for a while.

### Spatial locality

**If you used something, you will probably use its neighbours soon.** Instructions run one after another. Arrays are walked element by element. Fields of a struct are read together.

A cache exploits spatial locality by moving data in fixed-size blocks called **cache lines**, not single bytes. This module normally assumes **64-byte lines** and 4-byte ints; real line sizes vary, including 128-byte examples. A fill supplies other ints in the same line, not necessarily the next 15: that depends on the accessed int's position. Later accesses still have lookup costs.

```
 one 64-byte line = 8 x 8-byte doubles
 +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
 | d0 | d1 | d2 | d3 | d4 | d5 | d6 | d7 |
 +----+----+----+----+----+----+----+----+
   ^ read d0: miss, whole line fetched
     d1..d7: hits
```

> [!example] Summing an array
> Summing 1,000,000 4-byte ints walks 4 MB in order. For a line-aligned array, a cold demand-only cache with no interfering evictions fills 62,500 lines: 6.25% misses over 1,000,000 scalar loads. An unaligned start can add a line. Prefetching and interference change demand miss counts.

## Hits, misses and the working set

Some vocabulary used throughout this module:

- **Hit**: the data is in this level. **Miss**: it is not, and the request goes to the next level down.
- **Hit rate** = hits / accesses. **Miss rate** = 1 − hit rate.
- **Miss penalty**: the extra time a miss costs (the time to get the line from below).
- **Working set**: the data a program touches over a short window of time. Fitting in a level makes reuse possible, but set conflicts, other activity, coherence and replacement policy can still evict data. Exceeding capacity can increase misses.

The working set is why performance graphs often show **cliffs**. A carefully controlled repeated-access benchmark may show transitions near cache capacities. Streaming bandwidth, prefetching and access dependencies can make the curve quite different.

```
time per
access
  ^                          ______ DRAM
  |                  _______/
  |          _______/  L3
  |  _______/ L2
  |__/ L1
  +--------------------------> size
    32K    1M         32M
```

## Seeing locality in code

The same amount of work can have very different locality. Both functions below add up the same list of numbers; only the order differs.

```python
import random

N = 10_000_000
data = list(range(N))

def in_order():
    total = 0
    for i in range(N):
        total += data[i]
    return total

order = list(range(N))
random.shuffle(order)

def shuffled():
    total = 0
    for i in order:
        total += data[i]
    return total
```

In CPython, a list contains references to objects. Sequentially reading the reference array has spatial locality; shuffled indices scatter those accesses and can increase cache misses. Object allocation, shared objects, interpreter work, the extra index array and cache size affect the result. Run a controlled benchmark rather than assuming a fixed slowdown.

> A universal 5–10× slowdown and interpreter nanoseconds-per-iteration figure are omitted because no matching runtime, machine and benchmark were verified.

## Real-world consequences

- **Arrays can improve traversal locality compared with scattered linked lists**, even at the same big-O complexity. A dependent `next` pointer limits when the next demand address becomes known; whether it misses depends on placement, residency and prefetch capabilities.
- **B-trees can reduce serial node accesses compared with binary trees** for large indexes. A B-tree node is sized to hold many keys in a few cache lines (or one disk page), so each visited node can provide several nearby keys. A node may span several lines; cache misses depend on residency and search layout.
- **Hot loops should be small.** Instructions are cached too (in a separate L1 instruction cache). Huge unrolled or inlined code can overflow it.
- **Data size matters.** Using `int32` instead of `int64` fits twice as many integers per line; packing one-byte booleans into bits fits eight times as many flags, excluding layout overhead.

## Pitfalls

- **Assuming the big-O tells the whole story.** Two O(n) algorithms can differ by 10× because one streams memory and the other jumps around.
- **Benchmarking with tiny inputs.** If the test data fits in L1, you are measuring the fast path. Production data that spills to DRAM behaves differently.
- **Assuming 64-byte lines everywhere.** Line sizes vary by processor and cache level. Query the target (`sysctl hw.cachelinesize` on macOS, `getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE` on Linux) rather than hard-coding it in portable code.

## Key takeaways
- Distance, storage technology and lookup cost motivate a hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3, DRAM, storage.
- Exact latency ratios depend on hardware, load and access pattern; measure them rather than assuming a universal table.
- Temporal locality (reuse soon) is exploited by keeping recent data; spatial locality (neighbours soon) by moving whole cache lines, 64 bytes in the main examples here.
- Working-set capacity matters, but conflicts, replacement, prefetching and interference also determine hit rates.
- Data layout and access order can matter as much as algorithmic complexity.

questions.prompt: In a C loop `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) total += a[i];`, assume valid bounds and no arithmetic overflow. The scalar accumulator total is reused each iteration. Which kind of locality does that reuse illustrate?

options.text: Spatial locality
options.explanation: Spatial locality is about touching *neighbouring* addresses. `total` is the same address every time, which is reuse, not neighbourliness. The walk over `a[i]` is the spatial part.

options.text: Temporal locality
options.explanation: Correct. The same location is used again and again within a short time, so keeping it in a register or L1 pays off on every iteration.

options.text: No locality, because it changes value each iteration
options.explanation: Locality is about *addresses*, not values. The value changes but the location is the same, which is exactly temporal locality.

options.text: Sequential locality only
options.explanation: Sequential access is a special case of spatial locality (walking consecutive addresses). `total` does not move through memory at all.

questions.workedExample: The scalar accumulator is reused over a short interval: temporal locality. If kept in memory, its accesses revisit the same object; an optimiser may instead retain it in a register. The array walk separately illustrates spatial locality. This does not imply that a Python integer object stays at one fixed address during repeated addition.

questions.prompt: A cold cache with 64-byte lines sits in front of a loop that reads an array of 4,096 `double`s (8 bytes each) once, in order. Assume the array starts on a line boundary, each read miss allocates a line, and there is no prefetching or interfering access. how many cache misses occur?

options.explanation: That would be one miss per element, which ignores that each miss brings in a whole 64-byte line holding 8 doubles.
64 is the line size in bytes, not the number of lines. The array is 32 KiB, which is many lines.
Correct. 4,096 × 8 B = 32,768 B. 32,768 / 64 = 512 lines, and each line misses once (on its first element) then hits 7 times.
8 is the number of doubles per line, i.e. the number of accesses each miss serves, not the miss count.

questions.workedExample:
1. Array size: 4,096 × 8 B = 32,768 B (32 KiB).
2. Lines touched: 32,768 / 64 = **512**.
3. Each line misses on its first access (a compulsory miss) and the next 7 doubles in it hit.
4. Miss rate = 512 / 4,096 = 1/8 = **12.5%**.

```
line 0: d0 MISS d1..d7 hit
line 1: d8 MISS d9..d15 hit
...
512 lines -> 512 misses
```

With 4-byte ints instead, each line would hold 16 values and the miss rate would halve to 6.25%.

questions.prompt: Which list puts these in order from fastest to slowest typical access latency?

options.text: L1, L2, DRAM, L3, SSD
options.explanation: In the conventional hierarchy being compared, an L3 hit is normally quicker than a DRAM access.

options.text: Registers, L1, L2, L3, DRAM, SSD
options.explanation: Correct for the conventional hierarchy: register operands, then increasingly distant cache levels, DRAM, and storage. Actual operation latencies are implementation-dependent; register-based operations do not all take zero cycles.

options.text: Registers, L2, L1, L3, DRAM, SSD
options.explanation: L1 is the smallest cache and closest to the execution units; it is the fastest cache, not L2.

options.text: L1, registers, L2, L3, SSD, DRAM
options.explanation: This reverses the conventional register/cache and DRAM/storage ordering. No fixed ratio applies to all systems.

questions.workedExample: The conventional ordering is registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → DRAM → SSD. Register access is part of instruction execution, not a universal zero-cycle memory load. Exact latency figures are absent because a specific processor, device and measurement have not been verified for this comparison.

questions.prompt: In a repeatedly warmed array-sum benchmark, time per element is flat to roughly 1 MiB, then rises. The CPU has 48 KiB L1d, 1.25 MiB L2 and 30 MiB L3. Which cache-capacity hypothesis is most consistent with the location of this change, and should be checked with measurements?

options.text: Loss of effective L2 residency, increasing accesses served from lower levels
options.explanation: Correct as a hypothesis. The change is near the stated L2 capacity; competing data and mapping can reduce effective residency. The curve alone does not prove the cause.

options.text: The array no longer fits in L1
options.explanation: The change is much nearer the L2 size than the stated L1 size. Absence of a visible earlier transition does not prove L1 has no effect.

options.text: The array has started to spill to DRAM
options.explanation: A simple whole-working-set L3 capacity explanation is less consistent with the stated sizes, though individual DRAM misses can occur even below nominal L3 capacity.

options.text: The loop has become CPU-bound because the array is longer
options.explanation: Time *per element* normalises for array length. More elements alone would not change the per-element cost.

questions.workedExample: Compare the change location with the nominal sizes: roughly 1 MiB is closest to 1.25 MiB L2. This suggests testing an L2-residency explanation using cache counters and controlled repeated runs. Cache conflicts, competing data, prefetching, frequency and loop implementation can affect the curve. No exact latency or later performance cliff follows from capacity alone.

questions.prompt: Which of these changes would usually **improve spatial locality**? Select all that apply.

options.text: Replacing a linked list that is traversed often with a contiguous array
options.explanation: Correct. Array elements sit next to each other, so each fetched line holds several useful elements; list nodes can be anywhere in the heap.

options.text: Storing a counter that is only `0..1000` as `int16` rather than `int64` in a large array
options.explanation: Correct. Smaller elements mean four times as many values per 64-byte line, so a scan needs a quarter of the lines.

options.text: Visiting a 2D row-major array column by column instead of row by row
options.explanation: This makes it worse. In row-major layout, consecutive elements of a *row* are adjacent; walking down a column jumps a whole row each step.

options.text: Caching the result of an expensive function call so it is reused
options.explanation: That is reuse of the same data: temporal locality, not spatial.

options.text: Grouping the fields that are always read together into the same struct
options.explanation: Correct. Nearby hot fields are more likely to share useful cache lines, although size, alignment and padding determine the actual placement.

questions.workedExample:
Spatial locality = useful bytes that sit **next to each other**, so one 64-byte line serves several accesses.

- Array instead of list: neighbours are adjacent. ✔
- Smaller element type: more values per line (64/2 = 32 `int16` vs 64/8 = 8 `int64`). ✔
- Column-wise walk of a row-major array: each step skips a whole row, so each access can need a new line. ✘
- Memoising a function result: reuse of the same item, temporal. ✘
- Hot fields together: they can share fetched lines, depending on layout. ✔

questions.prompt: A cold linked list has scattered nodes beyond the cache capacity. Traversal follows one next-pointer chain. Why can it have less memory-level parallelism than a contiguous array scan?

options.text: Linked lists use more instructions per element
options.explanation: Extra instructions may contribute to runtime, but the key dependency in this question is that the next address comes from the current node.

options.text: Each next demand address depends on the previous node load, limiting overlap of demand misses
options.explanation: Correct. A single chain exposes a serial dependency. Array addresses can be computed independently. Prefetch support varies; not every pointer dereference must reach DRAM.

options.text: The CPU cache cannot store pointers
options.explanation: Caches can store pointer representations just as other bytes; pointer width is platform-dependent.

options.text: Linked lists are stored on disk rather than in RAM
options.explanation: Both live in RAM (the heap). The difference is layout and predictability, not the storage device.

questions.workedExample: For an array with fixed-size elements, the next address can be calculated without waiting for the previous element value. For `node = node->next`, the next demand address depends on the current load. Under the cold scattered-node assumptions, that dependency can limit overlap. Cache hits, node placement and specialised hardware prefetching can change the result. No measured slowdown ratio is asserted.

link.title: What every programmer should know about memory (LWN)

questions.prompt: Why don't chip designers simply make the L1 cache 64 MiB so that almost everything hits?

options.text: SRAM cannot be manufactured in sizes above 1 MiB
options.explanation: L3 caches are built from SRAM and reach tens or even ~100 MiB, so size alone is possible.

options.text: Large capacity competes with low hit latency, area and energy
options.explanation: Correct. More storage and selection/interconnect work create physical design trade-offs; banking and other techniques can mitigate them, but capacity is not free.

options.text: Larger caches always have higher miss rates
options.explanation: Bigger caches generally have *lower* miss rates. The problem is hit time, not miss rate.

options.text: The operating system limits L1 size
options.explanation: Software can influence use or partitioning on some platforms, but an OS limit is not the fundamental reason for small low-latency L1 designs.

questions.workedExample: L1 aims to supply frequently needed operands quickly. Increasing capacity can increase wire distance, selection complexity, area and energy. Designers balance those costs against miss reduction, often using multiple levels. Exact cycle counts are absent because they depend on the concrete design; there is no universal mandatory 4–5-cycle L1 or 40–70-cycle large cache.

questions.prompt: A CPython function scans a large list of ints in index order and in a shuffled order. Which statement about performance is most accurate?

options.text: Both take exactly the same time because the same values are added
options.explanation: Equal values and operation counts do not guarantee equal memory behaviour or runtime.

options.text: Shuffling can reduce locality and increase cache misses; the actual slowdown requires measurement
options.explanation: Correct. CPython lists contain references, and a shuffled traversal can scatter both reference and object accesses. Object sharing, layout, caches and loop overhead affect the outcome.

options.text: The shuffled version is faster because random access spreads load across memory banks
options.explanation: Spreading accesses across banks does not establish an overall speedup; locality and dependencies also matter.

options.text: The in-order version is slower because Python must check bounds sequentially
options.explanation: Both forms must obey indexing semantics. There is no general sequential-only bounds-check penalty.

questions.workedExample: CPython list storage contains references to objects, which may be shared rather than one allocation per list entry. Sequential reference accesses have spatial locality. A shuffled index stream can add misses and its own overhead. Pointer width, object size and interpreter cost depend on the build and values, so no fixed speedup or nanoseconds-per-iteration claim is made.

questions.prompt: Loop A reads every element of an aligned cold 64 MiB int32 array; B reads every 16th element. Lines are 64 bytes. Assume each needed line reaches DRAM exactly once, both loops achieve the same effective DRAM bandwidth, and transfer time dominates all other costs. In this model, how does B's runtime compare with A's?

options.text: About 1/16 of A's time, because it does 1/16 of the loads
options.explanation: The model makes transferred lines, rather than load count, determine time. Both touch every line.

options.text: About the same as A's, because both loops touch every cache line once
options.explanation: Correct. 16 int32s × 4 B = 64 B, so B's stride is exactly one line. Both loops fetch all 1,048,576 lines; B just uses 4 bytes of each.

options.text: About 16 times longer than A, because strided access defeats caching
options.explanation: Under the stated equal-bandwidth model both transfer the same bytes. Real code can differ if those assumptions fail.

options.text: About half of A's time, because the prefetcher fetches pairs of lines
options.explanation: The model already specifies equal effective bandwidth and one transfer per needed line; pair prefetching does not halve B's required bytes.

questions.workedExample: There are 64 MiB / 64 B = 1,048,576 lines. A reads 16 ints per line; B's stride is 16 × 4 = 64 B, touching one int in every line. Both transfer 64 MiB. Equal effective bandwidth and transfer-dominated runtime therefore give approximately equal times. Without those explicit assumptions, equal line counts alone do not determine runtime.

questions.prompt: Compare model caches A with 128-byte lines and B with 64-byte lines. An aligned cold array of 1,000,000 eight-byte doubles is read sequentially. Assume each needed line is filled once, with no extra traffic. How many fills are required in A versus B?

options.explanation: Correct: 8,000,000 / 128 = 62,500 and 8,000,000 / 64 = 125,000. The alignment and one-fill assumptions make the count exact.

options.text: 125,000 on both, since the data size is the same
options.explanation: Line size changes how many lines the same bytes occupy. The bytes are the same; the number of fills is not.

options.text: 1,000,000 on both, one per element
options.explanation: Each fill brings in 16 doubles (128 B) or 8 doubles (64 B), so most loads hit.
This swaps them: the *larger* 128-byte line needs *fewer* fills.

questions.workedExample: The array occupies 8,000,000 bytes. Cache A needs 8,000,000 / 128 = 62,500 fills; B needs 8,000,000 / 64 = 125,000. Both transfer the same useful array bytes in this aligned model. Larger lines can waste bandwidth on sparse accesses and enlarge the region affected by false sharing. These are model line sizes, not claims about entire processor families.

questions.prompt: A large RAM index is searched using either a balanced binary search tree with scattered nodes or a B-tree storing many keys per node. Which statements explain why the B-tree can improve cache behaviour? Select all that apply.

options.text: Larger fanout can reduce the number of nodes visited
options.explanation: Correct. A well-filled B-tree has more children per node, so it can have fewer levels than a balanced binary tree with the same number of keys.

options.text: Scattered binary-tree nodes can require dependent line fetches during descent
options.explanation: Correct. Each next node address depends on the current node; whether that access misses depends on cache state and placement.

options.text: Comparisons inside a B-tree node are free because they happen in DRAM
options.explanation: Comparisons happen in the CPU, on data already loaded into cache. They are cheap because the node's keys arrived together, not because DRAM computes them.

options.text: A B-tree changes the big-O of search from O(log n) to O(1)
options.explanation: Both balanced structures have logarithmic search depth. Layout, fanout and the cost per node affect practical performance.

questions.workedExample: A balanced binary tree with 100 million keys has depth on the order of log2(10^8) ≈ 26.6. An idealised fanout of 32 suggests a scale of log32(10^8) ≈ 5.3 levels; actual integer height depends on occupancy and node structure. Each B-tree node can occupy multiple lines, including child pointers. Fewer nodes can reduce serial dependent misses, but neither an exact DRAM round-trip count nor a speedup is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Cache organisation and address breakdown
lessons.summary: How a cache decides where a line can live, splitting an address into tag, index and offset, direct-mapped vs set-associative vs fully associative, the three Cs of misses, and replacement policies.
lessons.body:
A cache holds copies of memory lines. The lookup must determine whether the requested bytes are present. The conventional organisations below use address-derived indexing and tag comparison to locate possible entries efficiently. Exact lookup pipelines and latency vary.

## Lines, sets and ways

Three numbers describe a cache:

- **Capacity** C: total data bytes (e.g. 32 KiB).
- **Line size** B: bytes per line (e.g. 64).
- **Associativity** E: how many places (**ways**) a given line may go.

From these, the number of lines is C / B, and the lines are grouped into **sets** of E ways each:

```
 sets S = C / (B x E)
```

A memory line maps to exactly **one set**, but may sit in **any way** within that set.

| Organisation | Ways per set | Sets |
|---|---|---|
| Direct-mapped | 1 | C / B |
| E-way set-associative | E | C / (B·E) |
| Fully associative | all lines | 1 |

## Splitting the address

For this conventional byte-addressed, modulo-indexed model, the address is split into three fields. Hashed and skewed mappings need different indexing rules. For an address of *m* bits:

```
 |<-------------- m bits -------------->|
 +------------------+-----------+-------+
 |       tag        |   index   |offset |
 +------------------+-----------+-------+
   t = m - s - b       s bits    b bits
```

- **Offset** (b bits, b = log2 B): which byte within the line.
- **Index** (s bits, s = log2 S): which set to look in.
- **Tag** (the remaining t = m − s − b bits): stored alongside each line, and compared to tell apart the many memory lines that share a set.

The line size B and set count S must be powers of two for this simple bit-field split. Capacity C and way count E need not be: 48 KiB with 12 ways and 64-byte lines still has 64 sets.

A lookup then goes:

1. Use the **index** to select one set.
2. Compare the address's **tag** against the stored tag of every way in that set, in parallel. A way hits if its tag matches *and* its **valid bit** is set.
3. On a hit, use the **offset** to pick the bytes out of the line.

### Worked example 1: a small direct-mapped cache

A 1 KiB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte lines and 32-bit addresses.

1. Lines = 1024 / 16 = 64. Direct-mapped, so sets = 64.
2. Offset b = log2 16 = **4** bits.
3. Index s = log2 64 = **6** bits.
4. Tag t = 32 − 6 − 4 = **22** bits.

Now break down address `0x00001A2C`:

```
 0x1A2C = 0001 1010 0010 1100
 offset = low 4 bits    = 1100   = 12
 index  = next 6 bits   = 100010 = 34
 tag    = remaining     = 000110 = 6
```

So byte 12 of the line in set 34, with tag `0x6`. A quicker way: offset = addr mod 16 = 12; index = (addr div 16) mod 64 = 418 mod 64 = 34; tag = addr div 1024 = 6.

### Worked example 2: an L1-style model

Assume 32 KiB, 8 ways, 64-byte lines and 48-bit physical addresses. The tag calculation uses physical addresses; a 48-bit virtual address is not generally its physical tag.

1. Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512.
2. Sets = 512 / 8 = **64**.
3. Offset = log2 64 = **6** bits; index = log2 64 = **6** bits.
4. Tag = 48 − 6 − 6 = **36** bits.

Address `0x7FFE12345678`. The low 12 bits are `0x678` = `0110 0111 1000`:

```
 offset = 111000   = 56
 index  = 011001   = 25
 tag    = addr >> 12 = 0x7FFE12345
```

> [!tip] Hex shortcut
> When offset + index is a multiple of 4 bits, read the fields straight off the hex digits. Here offset + index = 12 bits = the last three hex digits (`678`), so the tag is everything before them: `0x7FFE12345`.

Notice that index + offset is exactly 12 bits, the size of a 4 KiB page offset. That is not a coincidence. It lets the L1 pick the set using address bits that are the same in the virtual and physical address, so the set lookup can start while the TLB translates the rest (a *virtually indexed, physically tagged* or VIPT cache; translation itself is covered in the OS subject). It is one reason a design might grow L1 by adding ways: 48 KiB with 12 ways also gives 64 sets. Other geometries can use other alias-management techniques.

## Direct-mapped: simple but fragile

Each line has exactly one home. Lookup is fast (one tag compare) and cheap in hardware. The weakness is **conflict**: two hot lines whose addresses share an index keep evicting each other, even if the rest of the cache is empty.

Take a tiny 128-byte cache with 16-byte lines (8 lines) and this trace, with an initially empty cache, demand-only reads and no interference:

```
 0x00 0x04 0x80 0x00 0x84 0x10 0x90 0x10
```

Direct-mapped, 8 sets: offset 4 bits, index 3 bits. `0x00` and `0x80` both have index 0 (tags 0 and 1); `0x10` and `0x90` both have index 1.

| Addr | Set | Tag | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 0 | 0 | miss |
| 0x04 | 0 | 0 | hit |
| 0x80 | 0 | 1 | miss (evicts 0) |
| 0x00 | 0 | 0 | miss (evicts 1) |
| 0x84 | 0 | 1 | miss |
| 0x10 | 1 | 0 | miss |
| 0x90 | 1 | 1 | miss |
| 0x10 | 1 | 0 | miss |

**1 hit in 8**, with six of the eight lines sitting empty the whole time.

## Set-associative: the usual compromise

Make the same 128 bytes **2-way**: 4 sets of 2 ways. Now the index is 2 bits; the tag occupies address-width minus 6 bits (2 tag bits if addresses are 8 bits). `0x00` (tag 0) and `0x80` (tag 2) both go to set 0, but there are two ways, so they coexist. With LRU replacement:

| Addr | Set | Tag | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 0 | 0 | miss |
| 0x04 | 0 | 0 | hit |
| 0x80 | 0 | 2 | miss |
| 0x00 | 0 | 0 | hit |
| 0x84 | 0 | 2 | hit |
| 0x10 | 1 | 0 | miss |
| 0x90 | 1 | 2 | miss |
| 0x10 | 1 | 0 | hit |

**4 hits in 8.** The remaining misses are all first-time (compulsory) misses. Making it fully associative would not help this trace any further.

The price of associativity is hardware: E tag comparators working in parallel, a multiplexer to choose the hitting way, and replacement state. More ways usually means slightly higher hit time and power. Exact associativities depend on the named cache.

> A generic L1/L2/L3 associativity table is omitted because the earlier ranges were not verified against a representative set of specified processors.

## The three Cs of misses

Classifying misses tells you what would fix them:

- **Compulsory** (cold): the first access to a line. Prefetching can turn a first demand access into a hit; changing line size or avoiding accesses also changes the count.
- **Capacity**: the working set is bigger than the cache. In the conventional three-C classification, a previously seen line also misses in a fully associative LRU reference cache of the same capacity and line size. Fix with a bigger cache or better locality (blocking).
- **Conflict**: a previously seen line misses here but hits in that fully associative reference cache, often because competing lines share a set. Fix with more associativity, or by changing addresses (padding).

Multicore systems add a fourth C, **coherence** misses, when another core invalidated your copy (see the coherence lesson).

## Replacement: choosing a victim

In a set-associative cache, allocating a new line into a full set requires a victim; a bypassed or no-write-allocate access need not allocate.

- **LRU**: evict the least recently used way. Exact LRU for 8 ways needs to track an ordering of 8 items per set, which is costly.
- **Pseudo-LRU (tree-PLRU)**: for a power-of-two E, a binary tree of E − 1 bits per set (7 bits for 8 ways) points roughly away from recent accesses. It uses less state than a full ordering, but can choose a different victim from true LRU.
- **RRIP-style policies**: give each line a small "re-reference prediction" counter so that lines that were used only once (a streaming scan) are evicted before reused lines. Such policies can resist scans; a particular processor’s policy requires implementation documentation.
- **Random** (pseudo-random): choose a victim using a random or pseudo-random mechanism. This can avoid maintaining a recency order; effectiveness is trace-dependent.

## Storage overhead

The data array is not the whole cache. Each line also stores its tag, a valid bit and (for a write-back cache) a dirty bit, plus replacement bits per set. For the 32 KiB 8-way example: 36 tag + 1 valid + 1 dirty = 38 bits per line, × 512 lines = 19,456 bits = 2,432 bytes, about 7.4% on top of the 32 KiB of data (before replacement and coherence state).

## Pitfalls

- **Power-of-two strides.** In the 64-set,64-byte-line model, strides divisible by 4,096 bytes retain the same set index. An 8-way set holds only eight such lines. Padding can spread rows across sets, but whether it prevents thrashing depends on the new stride and working set. (The friendly-code lesson works through this.)
- **Forgetting the tag bits shrink as the cache grows.** Doubling the number of sets moves one bit from tag to index.
- **Mixing up KB and KiB.** KiB denotes a binary unit: 32 KiB = 32,768 bytes; KB denotes 1,000 bytes when used in the SI sense.

## Key takeaways
- sets = capacity / (line size × ways); offset = log2(line size), index = log2(sets), tag = the rest.
- Lookup: the index picks a set, all its tags are compared in parallel, the offset selects the bytes.
- Direct-mapped is fast but suffers conflict misses; set-associative is the standard compromise; fully associative placement removes set restrictions but can be costly to implement at large capacity.
- Misses are compulsory, capacity, conflict (and, on multicore, coherence); each has a different cure.
- Replacement may use tree-PLRU, RRIP-style, random or other policies; do not infer a processor’s exact policy from associativity alone.

questions.prompt: A cache has 64-byte lines. How many address bits form the **offset** field? Assume byte addressing and the simple contiguous offset/index/tag bit-field model.

options.explanation: 64 is the number of bytes in a line. The offset needs enough bits to *number* 64 bytes, which is log2 64.
8 bits could address 256 bytes within a line, more than needed. Perhaps confusing bits with bytes per word.
Correct. 2^6 = 64, so 6 bits select any byte within a 64-byte line.
12 bits is index + offset for a typical 64-set L1, not the offset alone.

questions.workedExample:
The offset picks one byte inside a line.

1. Bytes per line: 64.
2. Bits needed to number 0..63: log2 64 = **6**.
3. Check: 6 bits give values 000000 to 111111 = 0 to 63. ✔

General rule: offset bits = log2(line size). 32 B → 5, 64 B → 6, 128 B → 7.

questions.prompt: In a **direct-mapped** cache, how many different cache locations can a given memory line be placed in?

options.text: Exactly one
options.explanation: Correct. The index bits pick a set, and in a direct-mapped cache each set has a single way, so there is only one possible home.

options.text: Any location, chosen by the replacement policy
options.explanation: That describes a *fully associative* cache, where there is one set containing every line.

options.text: One of E locations within its set
options.explanation: That is an E-way set-associative cache. Direct-mapped is the special case E = 1.

options.text: It depends on the size of the line
options.explanation: Line size changes how many lines there are, not how many places one line may go.

questions.workedExample:
Think of associativity as "ways per set":

| Organisation | Places per line |
|---|---|
| Direct-mapped | 1 |
| E-way | E |
| Fully associative | all |

Direct-mapped = 1-way. The index field computes the single slot, so there is no choice to make and no replacement policy is needed: an allocating miss replaces the valid occupant of that slot, if any.

questions.prompt: How many **sets** does a 32 KiB, 8-way set-associative cache with 64-byte lines have? Assume byte addressing and the simple contiguous offset/index/tag bit-field model.

options.explanation: 512 is the number of *lines* (32,768 / 64). The lines are grouped 8 to a set.
Correct. 32,768 / 64 = 512 lines; 512 / 8 ways = 64 sets.
8 is the number of ways per set, not the number of sets.
This divides 32,768 by 8 (the ways) but forgets to divide by the line size.

questions.workedExample:
Use sets = capacity / (line size × ways):

```
32,768 / (64 x 8)
= 32,768 / 512
= 64 sets
```

So the index field is log2 64 = 6 bits, and with a 6-bit offset that is 12 bits total, which neatly matches a 4 KiB page offset.

options.explanation: Correct. Offset = 0x1A2C mod 16 = 12; index = (6,700 div 16) mod 64 = 418 mod 64 = 34; tag = 6,700 div 1,024 = 6.

options.text: Tag 0x1A, index 2, offset 12
options.explanation: This splits on hex digits (4-bit boundaries) as if the index were 4 bits. The cache has 64 sets, so the index is 6 bits and does not line up with hex digits.

options.text: Tag 0x6, index 12, offset 34

options.text: Tag 0x1, index 162, offset 12

1. Lines = 1,024 / 16 = 64; direct-mapped, so 64 sets.
2. Field widths: offset 4, index 6, tag 32 − 10 = 22.
3. 0x1A2C in binary:

0001 1010 0010 1100
tag    |index |off
000110 100010 1100
  = 6    = 34  = 12

4. Check with arithmetic: 0x1A2C = 6,700.

options.text: Set 103, tag 0x7FFE12345

options.text: Set 25, tag 0x7FFE12345
options.explanation: Correct. Offset + index = 12 bits = the last three hex digits, 0x678 = 0110 0111 1000. Offset = 111000 = 56, index = 011001 = 25, tag = everything above, 0x7FFE12345.

options.text: Set 56, tag 0x7FFE12345
options.explanation: 56 is the *offset* (the low 6 bits). The index is the next 6 bits up.

options.text: Set 25, tag 0x1FFF848D15

questions.workedExample:
1. Lines = 32,768 / 64 = 512; sets = 512 / 8 = 64.
2. Offset 6 bits, index 6 bits, tag 48 − 12 = 36 bits.
3. Index + offset = 12 bits = 3 hex digits: `678`.

```
0x678 = 0110 0111 1000
index  = 011001 = 25
offset = 111000 = 56
```

4. Tag = the remaining 9 hex digits: `0x7FFE12345` (36 bits).

options.text: Tag 29, index 11, offset 6
options.explanation: Correct. 2 MiB / 64 B = 32,768 lines; / 16 ways = 2,048 sets = 2^11. Tag = 46 − 11 − 6 = 29.

options.text: Tag 25, index 15, offset 6
options.explanation: 15 index bits would number 32,768 sets, which is the number of *lines*. Divide by the 16 ways first.

options.text: Tag 33, index 7, offset 6
options.explanation: 7 index bits would mean 128 sets. That divides by 256 rather than 16 somewhere.

options.text: Tag 24, index 16, offset 6
options.explanation: 16 bits of index means 65,536 sets, more than the cache has lines.

options.explanation: 3 is the answer for a 2-way version of the same 64-byte cache, where 0x00/0x40 and 0x10/0x54 can coexist. Direct-mapped, they evict each other.
0x18 is in the same line as 0x14 (both 0x10–0x1F), which is still resident when 0x18 arrives, so there is at least one hit.
Correct. Only 0x18 hits. 0x00 and 0x40 fight over set 0; 0x14 and 0x54 fight over set 1, so each return finds its line evicted.
0x04 looks like a hit (same line as 0x00), but 0x40 evicted that line from set 0 in between.

questions.workedExample:
Offset 4 bits, index 2 bits, tag 2 bits. Index = (addr div 16) mod 4.

| Addr | Set | Tag | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x00 | 0 | 0 | miss |
| 0x14 | 1 | 0 | miss |
| 0x40 | 0 | 1 | miss, evicts tag 0 |
| 0x04 | 0 | 0 | miss, evicts tag 1 |
| 0x18 | 1 | 0 | **hit** |
| 0x54 | 1 | 1 | miss, evicts tag 0 |
| 0x10 | 1 | 0 | miss |

1 hit. As a 2-way cache (2 sets), 0x04, 0x18 and 0x10 would all hit: 3 hits. The extra misses here are conflict misses.

questions.prompt: Using first touch for compulsory misses and a same-capacity fully associative LRU reference cache to distinguish capacity from conflict misses, which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Doubling associativity (same capacity) can reduce conflict misses
options.explanation: Correct. Conflict misses happen when too many hot lines share a set; more ways per set lets them coexist.

options.text: Doubling associativity eliminates compulsory misses
options.explanation: Associativity does not remove the first touch of a line in a cold demand-only trace. Prefetching can move the miss off the demand path, and different line sizes or access patterns can change the number of distinct lines touched.

options.text: A miss also occurring in the same-capacity fully associative LRU reference is capacity or compulsory
options.explanation: Correct under the stated classification. The replacement rule must be specified; placement freedom alone does not specify a trace outcome.

options.text: Capacity misses can be reduced by restructuring loops so the working set fits (blocking)
options.explanation: Correct. Blocking shrinks the data touched between reuses so it fits in the cache.

options.text: Conflict misses cannot happen in a set-associative cache
options.explanation: They can, whenever more than E hot lines map to one set, e.g. a power-of-two stride hitting a single set of an 8-way cache.

questions.workedExample: Compulsory: first touch of a line. For subsequent misses, compare with the same-capacity fully associative LRU reference: a reference miss is classified as capacity; a reference hit identifies a conflict miss. More associativity or suitable layout can reduce some conflicts; blocking can reduce reuse distance. These are possible improvements, not guarantees that every trace improves monotonically.

questions.prompt: The 32 KiB, 8-way, 64-byte-line, 48-bit-physical-address L1 is write-back. Each line stores its tag, a valid bit and a dirty bit. Assume the same simple indexing model and ideal bit packing. Ignoring replacement, coherence, ECC/parity and array-layout overhead, how much extra storage does that metadata need?

options.text: 2,432 bytes (about 7.4% of the data capacity)
options.explanation: Correct. Tag = 36 bits; per line 36 + 1 + 1 = 38 bits. 512 lines × 38 = 19,456 bits = 2,432 bytes; 2,432 / 32,768 ≈ 7.4%.

options.text: 512 bytes (one byte per line)
options.explanation: A tag here is 36 bits, far more than one byte, so this badly undercounts.

options.text: 304 bytes
options.explanation: This counts 38 bits for each of the 64 *sets*, but every line (every way) has its own tag, valid and dirty bits.

options.text: 2,560 bytes
options.explanation: This uses 40 bits per line, i.e. a 38-bit tag. With 6 index and 6 offset bits removed from 48, the tag is 36.

questions.workedExample:
1. Sets = 64, so index 6 bits; offset 6 bits.
2. Tag = 48 − 6 − 6 = 36 bits.
3. Metadata per line = 36 + 1 (valid) + 1 (dirty) = 38 bits.
4. Lines = 512.

```
512 x 38 = 19,456 bits
19,456 / 8 = 2,432 bytes
2,432 / 32,768 = 7.4%
```

A design may add replacement state (for example, 7 tree-PLRU bits per 8-way set), coherence bits and ECC/parity. Physical array layout also adds implementation-dependent overhead.

questions.prompt: Two arrays of `double`s, `a` at `0x10000` and `b` at `0x18000`, are read alternately: `a[0], b[0], a[1], b[1], ...` for 64 elements each. Assume 8-byte doubles, an initially empty 32 KiB cache with 64-byte lines, simple modulo indexing, read allocation, no prefetching and no other accesses. What miss rate do you get if it is direct-mapped, and if it is 2-way with LRU?

options.text: 12.5% for both
options.explanation: This would be true if `a[i]` and `b[i]` used different sets. They are 32 KiB apart, exactly the size of a direct-mapped cache, so they land in the same set.

options.text: 100% direct-mapped; 12.5% 2-way
options.explanation: Correct. Direct-mapped: `a[i]` and `b[i]` share a set and evict each other on every access, so all 128 accesses miss. 2-way: both lines fit in the set, so each line misses once and serves 8 doubles: 16 misses / 128 = 12.5%.

options.text: 50% direct-mapped; 0% 2-way
options.explanation: Even a perfect cache has compulsory misses: 16 distinct lines must each be fetched once, so 2-way cannot reach 0%.

options.text: 100% for both
options.explanation: Two ways are enough for two competing lines, so the 2-way cache stops the ping-pong.

questions.workedExample:
1. 0x18000 − 0x10000 = 0x8000 = 32 KiB, the direct-mapped cache's size. Addresses that differ by a multiple of the cache size share an index.
2. **Direct-mapped** (512 sets): `a[i]` loads a line into set *k*; `b[i]` maps to set *k* too and evicts it; `a[i+1]` (same line as `a[i]`) misses again... Every one of the 128 accesses misses.
3. **2-way** (256 sets, 16 KiB per way): still same set, but 2 ways hold one line of `a` and one of `b`.
   - Lines touched: 64 × 8 B / 64 B = 8 per array, 16 total.
   - Misses = 16, accesses = 128 → **12.5%**.

This is the classic conflict-miss pathology, and why compilers and allocators sometimes pad arrays.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical VIPT L1d with 64-byte lines and 4 KiB pages grows from 32 KiB/8-way to 48 KiB/12-way, retaining simple bit-field indexing. What advantage does keeping the number of sets unchanged provide?

options.text: More sets would need more offset bits, breaking the 64-byte line size
options.explanation: The number of sets affects the *index*, not the offset. Line size alone sets the offset.

options.text: Keeping 64 sets keeps index + offset at 12 bits, inside the 4 KiB page offset, so the set can be selected from untranslated address bits in parallel with the TLB lookup
options.explanation: Correct. Page-offset bits are unchanged by translation. A set index extending above that offset needs additional alias-handling constraints or mechanisms; adding ways avoids that issue in this model.

options.text: Fully associative caches are faster, so more ways always means faster hits
options.explanation: More ways do not guarantee faster hits: comparisons, selection and energy can grow. The relevant advantage here is keeping the set index within the page offset.

options.text: 12 is a power of two
options.explanation: 12 is not a power of two. Simple bit-field indexing requires power-of-two line size and set count, not necessarily ways or total capacity.

questions.workedExample: 48 KiB / (64 B × 12) = 64 sets. Six set bits plus six offset bits fit in the unchanged 12-bit offset of a 4 KiB page. A 48 KiB/6-way alternative would have 128 sets and use bit 12 in the index. Its virtual bit 12 is available early, but need not equal physical bit 12, so aliases require additional handling. Adding ways is one design choice, not the only way to build a larger VIPT cache. A vendor-generation catalogue is absent because those precise configurations have not been reliably verified here.

lessons.title: Write policies and AMAT
lessons.summary: What happens on a store (write-through vs write-back, write-allocate vs no-write-allocate), how inclusion works between levels, and how to calculate average memory access time and stall CPI in an explicit blocking-cache model.
lessons.body:
Reads are the easy half of caching: if the line is present, return it; if not, fetch it. Writes raise harder questions. When a store hits in L1, does memory get updated now or later? When a store misses, do we bother fetching the line at all? The answers change how much traffic flows between levels, and that changes performance.

The second half of this lesson turns all of this into one number: the **average memory access time** (AMAT), and from it the cost in cycles per instruction.

## On a write hit: write-through or write-back

### Write-through

Every store updates the cached copy and must be propagated to the next level. A **write buffer** can defer or merge those updates, so the next level need not reflect a pending store immediately.

- A clean write-through line does not need a dirty eviction write-back; pending buffered writes still must complete correctly.
- Without write merging, one million issued stores send one million writes downstream. Merging can reduce that traffic.
- A full write buffer can stall further stores.

### Write-back

A store updates the cache line and marks it **dirty**. Modified data is propagated when required, for example on dirty eviction, explicit write-back, or a coherence request; eviction is not the only trigger.

- Repeated local writes can avoid repeated downstream data writes while the core retains ownership. They still consume execution/cache resources.
- In the simple allocate-on-miss model, replacing a dirty victim requires preserving its data and fetching the incoming line.
- A lower cache or DRAM may hold stale data, so coherent agents must obtain the current copy through the coherence mechanism. Non-coherent DMA requires the platform's cache-maintenance rules.

The following traffic example assumes no write merging, no intervening coherence requests, and one final eviction:

```
 write-through       write-back
 x=1 -> L1 and L2    x=1 -> L1 (dirty)
 x=2 -> L1 and L2    x=2 -> L1 (dirty)
 x=3 -> L1 and L2    x=3 -> L1 (dirty)
                     evict -> L2 gets 3
 3 writes to L2      1 write to L2
```

Write-back is common for ordinary cacheable memory, but policies depend on the processor, cache level, memory type, and instruction. A processor-by-processor policy catalogue is absent here because those specific configurations have not been reliably verified.

## On a write miss: allocate or not

- **Write-allocate**: allocate a cache line on a store miss, then update it. A partial-line store commonly fetches the old line; hardware may avoid that fetch for a complete overwrite. Good if you will read or write nearby data soon.
- **No-write-allocate** (write-around): send the write to the next level and leave the cache alone. Good for data you will not touch again.

The natural pairings are **write-back + write-allocate** (the usual choice) and **write-through + no-write-allocate**.

In a coherent fetch-on-write model, a store miss requests exclusive permission, often through a **read for ownership** (RFO) transaction that also obtains the line. Data may come from another cache rather than DRAM. A full-line overwrite may permit an implementation to omit the old-data fetch.

> [!example] Modelled traffic for overwriting 64 MiB
> Assume aligned 64-byte lines initially absent from all caches, no useful old data, no write-fetch elimination, and eventual write-back of every dirty line. Ordinary fetch-on-write stores read 64 MiB and write 64 MiB: **128 MiB** of DRAM data traffic.
> In an ideal full-line streaming-store path that avoids allocation/old-data reads, the corresponding data traffic is **64 MiB**. Real non-temporal instructions and library thresholds are implementation-specific; this is a traffic model, not a guarantee for every `memset` call.

## Inclusion between levels

These properties apply to the particular pair or collection of cache levels being discussed:

- **Inclusive**: presence in an included upper level implies presence in the lower level. The lower copy need not contain the newest bytes when an upper copy is dirty. Evicting the lower entry requires invalidating the included upper entries. Inclusion can help filter snoops, at the cost of duplicated capacity.
- **Exclusive**: a line is resident in only one of the specified levels. Their nominal capacities can therefore add without duplication between those levels; other caches and metadata remain separate concerns.
- **Neither inclusive nor exclusive (NINE)**: neither presence nor absence in one level guarantees the corresponding state in another. “Non-inclusive” alone does not necessarily rule out an exclusive design.

Specific processor-generation inclusion policies are not catalogued here because the necessary configuration-specific verification is unavailable in this lesson.



## Average memory access time

For the serial, blocking lookup model used here, AMAT is the expected service time of one memory access:

```
 AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty
```

Here the **hit time** is paid on every access (you always look in the cache first), and the **miss penalty** is the *extra* time when you miss.

### Worked example 1: one level

L1 hit time 4 cycles, miss rate 5%, miss penalty 100 cycles.

```
 AMAT = 4 + 0.05 x 100
      = 4 + 5
      = 9 cycles
```

The extra miss penalty contributes 5 cycles per access, versus 4 cycles for the lookup paid on **every** access. The hit-only contribution in the alternative weighted form is 0.95 × 4 = 3.8 cycles.

### Two conventions, same answer

Some books write AMAT = (hit rate × hit time) + (miss rate × total miss time), where the total miss time *includes* the initial lookup. With total miss time = 4 + 100 = 104:

```
 0.95 x 4 + 0.05 x 104 = 3.8 + 5.2 = 9
```

Same result. Mixing the conventions (using 100 as the total) gives 8.8, which is wrong. Always check whether a penalty includes the hit time.

### Worked example 2: two levels

In this serial model, the miss penalty of L1 is the incremental time spent accessing L2 and any lower level. The table uses incremental lookup times, not end-to-end latencies that already include earlier lookups.

| Level | Hit time | Local miss rate |
|---|---|---|
| L1 | 4 cycles | 5% |
| L2 | 12 cycles | 20% |
| DRAM | 200 cycles | - |

```
 L2 AMAT = 12 + 0.20 x 200 = 52
 AMAT    = 4 + 0.05 x 52
         = 4 + 2.6 = 6.6 cycles
```

### Local vs global miss rate

- **Local miss rate** of a level = its misses / accesses *that reach it*. L2's 20% is local: of the 5% of accesses that reach L2, 20% miss.
- **Global miss rate** = its misses / *all* CPU accesses. L2 global = 0.05 × 0.20 = **1%**.

These products describe the same stream of demand accesses filtered through successive levels, ignoring additional prefetch, write-back, and coherence traffic. Use local rates in the nested formula. A quoted L2 miss rate of "20%" sounds terrible but, here, only 1 access in 100 goes to DRAM.

### Worked example 3: three levels

L1: 4 cycles, 10% miss. L2: 14 cycles, 40% local miss. L3: 50 cycles, 25% local miss. DRAM: 300 cycles.

```
 L3 = 50 + 0.25 x 300 = 125
 L2 = 14 + 0.40 x 125 = 64
 L1 =  4 + 0.10 x 64  = 10.4 cycles
```

Global L3 miss rate = 0.10 × 0.40 × 0.25 = 1%.

The same recursion in Python:

```python
def amat(levels, memory_time):
    """levels: [(hit_time, local_miss)]
    from L1 downwards."""
    t = memory_time
    for hit, miss in reversed(levels):
        t = hit + miss * t
    return t

print(amat([(4, .05), (12, .20)], 200))
# 6.6
print(amat([(4, .10), (14, .40),
            (50, .25)], 300))
# 10.4
```

### Dirty evictions in the penalty

With write-back and no buffering, a miss that evicts a dirty line must write it back first. If 40% of victims are dirty and a write-back costs as much as a fetch (100 cycles):

```
 penalty = 100 + 0.4 x 100 = 140
 AMAT    = 4 + 0.05 x 140 = 11 cycles
```

A **write-back buffer** can hold the dirty victim while its write-back overlaps the fetch or later execution. The benefit depends on scheduling, available bandwidth, and buffer space; it is not guaranteed to recover a particular AMAT.

## From AMAT to CPI

Using the iron law (CPU time = instructions × CPI × cycle time), memory stalls add directly to CPI for a simple in-order core that blocks on misses:

```
 CPI = base CPI
     + (mem refs / instr) x miss rate
       x miss penalty
```

Assume base CPI already includes cache-hit execution cost and that miss penalties cannot overlap. With base CPI 1.0, 0.4 data references per instruction, L1d miss rate 5%, and an L1 miss penalty of 52 cycles (the L2 AMAT above):

```
 stalls = 0.4 x 0.05 x 52 = 1.04
 CPI    = 1.0 + 1.04 = 2.04
```

Half of all cycles are spent waiting for memory. Instruction fetches add their own term if the L1i misses.

## Trade-offs and pitfalls

- **AMAT is a model for blocking caches.** Out-of-order cores keep running independent instructions during a miss and can have many misses outstanding at once (**memory-level parallelism**). Ten overlapped 100-cycle misses do not cost 1,000 cycles. AMAT alone cannot reliably rank such designs or predict total stall time: dependency chains, overlap, bandwidth, and queueing can change the result.
- **Average hides the tail.** A loop with 99% hits can still be dominated by the 1% if those are DRAM misses.
- **Evaluate hit time and miss rate together.** In this model L1 lookup time is paid on every access; lower-level costs are weighted by how often accesses reach them. Which change matters most depends on the workload and trade-off.
- **Write-allocate can double traffic** for streaming writes; use streaming stores or library routines that do.

## Key takeaways
- Write-through propagates stores, possibly through a merging buffer; write-back tracks dirty data and propagates it when required, including eviction or coherence events.
- Write-allocate allocates a line on a store miss. A partial-line update often needs old bytes and exclusive permission; a full-line streaming path may avoid the old-data read.
- AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied recursively from the bottom up with local miss rates.
- Global miss rate = product of local miss rates down to that level.
- For non-overlapping blocking misses, stall CPI = references per instruction × miss rate × extra penalty; add it to a base CPI that already includes hits.
